task: Write one sentence of your own using the word plenitude. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know plenitude should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The new library opened with a plenitude of seats — window nooks, study pods, armchairs — so no student ever hovered waiting.
Enough stops short of plenitude — enough merely covers the need, with nothing left over to admire.
Plenty stops short of plenitude — plenty says you won't run out, while plenitude names fullness so complete it feels like a state of grace.

Bounty is abundance framed as a gift — nature's generosity or a giver's open hand, received with gratitude and gathered in. Plenitude needs no giver at all: it is the state of fullness itself, supply so complete that nothing feels missing.

Profusion is abundance in motion — quantity pouring out where everyone can see it, like confetti filling the air. Plenitude is the quieter condition all that pouring can produce: complete supply, calmly possessed. A profusion performs its abundance; a plenitude simply has it.

A cornucopia is the horn of plenty — an overflowing assortment of many different good things spilling out together: fruit, flowers, grain. Plenitude does not require variety; a plenitude of seats is simply seats enough for everyone, one kind of thing in complete supply.

Where this unit's plethora tips toward too many, plenitude stays glad: abundance with no complaint attached.

Plenitude, plethora, and surfeit all live in this unit, and they climb a scale of welcome: plenitude is abundance enjoyed; plethora is abundance become clutter — more than anyone can use; surfeit is abundance past the point of harm.
Say plenitude when the fullness is good news.

The aquifer survey changed the arithmetic.
Engineers found water enough for ten towns the size of Harwick, renewable each winter by the snowpack.

Fountains ran in the square, the school built a pool, and the fire brigade stopped charging for tank refills.
